title: The Sound of His Bat Was Like a Gunshot': Sangakkara Recalls the Day He Discovered Sooryavanshi
excerpt: Speaking on Sky Sports Cricket during the India-Ireland broadcast, the Rajasthan Royals director of cricket described a training-camp net session in Guwahati where a 14-year-old put Jofra Archer and Sandeep Sharma to the sword — and left even the fast bowlers stunned.
body:
Before Vaibhav Sooryavanshi became the youngest player ever auctioned in IPL history, before the 72 sixes and the Orange Cap and the India call-up, there was a side net in Guwahati where nobody wanted to bat.

Kumar Sangakkara remembers it vividly. Speaking on Sky Sports Cricket during India's first T20 International against Ireland in Belfast on Thursday, the Rajasthan Royals director of cricket and former Sri Lanka captain recalled the moment he first laid eyes on the teenager who would go on to rewrite IPL record books.

"I first saw Vaibhav when I came in for a two-week period to Guwahati," Sangakkara said. "There was this tiny, horrible little side net where the likes of Archer and Sandeep Sharma were bowling with the new ball, and no one really wanted to bat there."

Then a 14-year-old walked in and volunteered.

"I saw Vaibhav walk in and say, 'I'll bat.' Every time he hit the ball, I could hear the sound of his bat like a gunshot."

## Even Archer Could Only Laugh

What followed left even Rajasthan Royals' seasoned international fast bowlers lost for words. Sooryavanshi, barely a teenager and facing 90-mph thunderbolts from Jofra Archer, did not flinch. He attacked.



> **""He just put Archer to the sword; he put Sandeep Sharma to the sword," Sangakkara said."**


"He just put Archer to the sword; he put Sandeep Sharma to the sword," Sangakkara said. "So much so that at one time, I think Archer stopped and laughed. Because he was bowling quickly, and this 14-year-old kid was just treating him with absolute disdain."

The anecdote is remarkable not just for the audacity it describes but for the calibre of the witness. Sangakkara, one of the finest batsmen in cricket history with over 28,000 international runs across all formats, does not throw praise lightly. His immediate instinct was to walk straight to then-head coach Rahul Dravid — another batting great — and deliver his verdict.

"My feedback to Rahul, walking out, was: 'Yeah, ready to play anytime you want him to play. Kid's just incredible,'" Sangakkara added.

## A Season That Defied Belief

That assessment was spectacularly vindicated during IPL 2026. Sooryavanshi, now 15, finished the tournament as its highest run-scorer with 776 runs across 16 matches at an average of 48.50 and a jaw-dropping strike rate of 237.30. He hammered 72 sixes during the season — breaking Chris Gayle's long-standing record for the most sixes in a single IPL edition. He swept the individual awards: Orange Cap, Most Valuable Player, Emerging Player, Super Striker, and Most Sixes.

The left-hander from Samastipur in Bihar — a state with virtually no first-class cricket infrastructure — went from being a teenager picked up at the 2024 mega auction for ₹1.1 crore to being the most talked-about cricketer on the planet. His 15-ball fifty against CSK early in the season was the joint-third fastest in league history. By the tournament's end, he had made the extraordinary look routine.

## Waiting in the Wings in Belfast

Despite the clamour, Sooryavanshi did not feature in India's first T20I against Ireland, which the hosts won by 34 runs — Ireland's first-ever victory over India in any format. Shreyas Iyer, captaining India in his first T20I assignment, will be weighing whether to hand the teenager his debut in the second match on Sunday, or during the five-match T20I series against England that follows in July.

The 15-year-old's recent form with India A suggests he is ready: he smashed a record 11-ball half-century in a List A match, continuing the fearless approach that first caught Sangakkara's eye in that Guwahati net.

## From Bihar to the World

For the Indian diaspora watching from the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and beyond, Sooryavanshi's rise carries a particular resonance. It is the kind of story that transcends the sport — a teenager from a cricket backwater in eastern India, with raw talent so electrifying that it stopped a world-class fast bowler in his tracks, now standing on the threshold of international cricket.

The IPL, broadcast in over 120 countries and followed by millions of NRIs, has long been a showcase for young Indian talent. But few have arrived quite like this. And if Sangakkara's memory of that Guwahati afternoon is any guide, the best may still be ahead.

As the Rajasthan Royals' director of cricket put it: the kid was incredible then. The numbers say he still is.
